content: Thumb sucking is the act of placing the thumb into the mouth and rhythmically sucking on it for an extended period. This behavior can also involve other accessible parts of the body, such as the big toe. It is often perceived as soothing and therapeutic for the individual. Thumb sucking is most commonly observed in infants and young children. Babies naturally suck on objects, including pacifiers, as a self-soothing mechanism, and this behavior is considered a normal reflex in early childhood. While some adults also engage in thumb sucking, they typically do so in private due to feelings of embarrassment or shyness. Public thumb sucking by adults is rare and often stigmatized. Thumb sucking can begin as early as 15 weeks of fetal development in the womb, as the fetus develops the ability to move its digits. Before 12 weeks of gestation, the fetus’s fingers are still webbed. Most children gradually stop thumb sucking by the age of five, and it is uncommon for the habit to persist into adulthood. Some individuals may suck on both thumbs or their fingers, which is less common but similar in effect and treatment to thumb sucking. Thumb sucking can lead to dental problems, particularly if the habit persists beyond the eruption of permanent teeth. To discourage thumb sucking, some parents have historically used methods such as applying hot sauce or sour substances to the child’s thumb. However, these practices are not recommended by the American Dental Association (ADA) or the Association of Pediatric Dentists. In the 1950s, a device known as a hay-rake, consisting of sharp prongs cemented to a child’s teeth, was used to deter thumb sucking, though such methods are no longer considered appropriate. Most children naturally stop sucking their thumbs, pacifiers, or other objects between the ages of two and four, and no harm is typically done to their teeth or jaws during this time. However, if thumb sucking continues beyond the ages of six to eight, it may affect the shape of the oral cavity or the alignment of the teeth. The ADA provides several recommendations for addressing thumb sucking: Praise children when they refrain from thumb sucking, rather than scolding them when they engage in the behavior. If thumb sucking is a response to insecurity or a need for comfort, address the underlying cause of the anxiety and provide emotional support to the child. If the behavior is due to boredom, redirect the child’s attention with engaging activities. Involve older children in choosing a method to help them stop thumb sucking. Pediatric dentists can offer encouragement and explain the potential impact of thumb sucking on dental health. If other methods fail, gently remind the child of the habit by bandaging the thumb or placing a sock or glove on the hand at night. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the ADA both emphasize that thumb sucking is a natural reflex in early childhood. However, they note that the behavior may become a concern if it continues beyond the ages of six to eight or if it affects the development of the oral cavity and the alignment of teeth. Sigmund Freud viewed thumb sucking as a form of sexual expression and linked it to his studies of infantile sexuality. He suggested that intense thumb sucking could fully absorb a child’s attention, sometimes leading to sleep or, in rare cases, a motor reaction resembling an orgasm. Freud also noted that thumb sucking could be accompanied by the stimulation of other sensitive areas of the body, such as the genitals, and proposed that this behavior could evolve into masturbation as the child grows. In popular media, thumb sucking has been depicted in various ways. The 2005 film Thumbsucker, directed by Mike Mills, explores the life of a 17-year-old teenager who continues to suck his thumb. The movie is based on a 1999 novel of the same name by Walter Kirn. Additionally, Walt Disney Studio’s 1973 animated film Robin Hood portrays Prince John as an adult who sucks his thumb.
